newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: QUESTIONS RAISED IN SOUTH AFRICA OVER WINE ACCORD.
newsitem.headline: QUESTIONS RAISED IN SOUTH AFRICA OVER WINE ACCORD.

text.p: South Africa's competition board should probe an agreement signed this week between wine cooperative KWV and liquor wholesalers, the legal advisor to Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom said on Wednesday.

"I would advise him (Hanekom) to make sure the agreement is the subject of a competition board inquiry," lawyer Steven Goldblatt told Reuters, saying the accord appeared to mitigate against the entry of new players into the wine industry.
"It seems prima facie to fly in the face of a transparent, open and accessible market," Goldblatt said.
KWV spokesman Cassie du Plessis declined to comment on Goldblatt's remarks.

But he said the agreement in principle signed with the Cape Wine and Spirits Industry (CSWI) meant that the wholesalers' group would withdraw its efforts in court to block KWV from converting itself into a private company.
"There might be certain contracts emanating from this," du Plessis said, adding that details of the agreement still had to be finalised.

Hanekom has also brought a court action to block the KWV move, basing his action in part on the fact that KWV has used its position as a statutory industry regulator to accumulate assets at no business risk to itself.
KWV's court application to convert to a company and Hanekom's objection were both postponed on Wednesday to be heard in the Cape Town supreme court on April 2.

The CSWI -- which includes among others the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery , Distillers Corp Ltd , Douglas Green Bellingham, Gilbeys and Seagram -- initially opposed KWV's plan to become a private company on the grounds that it would pose unfair competition in the local market.
Sources close to the agreement signed this week said KWV had given the CSWI assurances that its marketing efforts would remain focused on exports, at least in the short term.

"All the infrastructure needed for KWV suddenly to have products in the domestic market -- lorries, distribution channels, marketing channels -- all these things cost an incredible amount of money if you start from scratch," one source said.
The sources said KWV believed its current activities were generating sufficient profits and that trying to break into the domestic market would not be attractive to the co-operative.
They said that because of a shortage of quality wine in South Africa, KWV did not have enough product to service its foreign customers.
KWV, with 4,400 winefarmer members, operates in about 50 countries but is barred by law from selling in Africa south of the equator unless its members agree.
It provides about 50 percent of the brandy sold in South Africa under various labels. According to court papers, KWV has accumulated assets of more than one billion rand ($230 million).
The Food and Allied Workers Union gave notice in court on Wednesday that it also intended to try to block KWV's attempts to become a private company.
A government-appointed commission recommended in February that the Wine and Spirits Control Act, which grants KWV its regulatory powers, be scrapped.
